newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan banks seen hit by rupee, repo changes.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan banks seen hit by rupee, repo changes.

text.p: Pakistani bank earnings will suffer after this week's rupee devaluation and hike in the central bank's repo rate, a research report said on Thursday.

"The financial sector as a whole will feel the pinch and we maintain our underweight recommendation, particularly on investment banks and leasing companies," said the report prepared by brokerage house KASB & Co.
State Bank of Pakistan governor Muhammad Yaqub devalued the rupee 7.86 percent against the dollar on Tuesday and raised the repurchase (repo) discount rate to 20 percent from 17.

He also unveiled a package of International Monetary Fund-inspired measures to stabilise the economy, avert any foreign exchange crisis and reduce Pakistan's yawning budget and current account deficits.
Yaqub said the government would narrow the budget deficit by 40 billion rupees ($995 million) through spending cuts and additional taxes in 1996/97 (July-June).
KASB & Co said banks would get higher fee-based earnings from any improvement in exports, which normally account for 20 to 25 percent of total bank revenues, due to the devaluation.

"We feel a short-term improvement in exports is likely, and banks would be able to capitalise on the immediate rise," it said. However, industrialists were sceptical that the lower rupee would cause a sustainable jump in export receipts.
The report said the rise in the repo rate would increase interbank borrowing costs for banks, especially for leasing companies and investment banks.
Banks might see profit margins suffer because they might not be able to pass on the higher borrowing cost to the corporate sector where demand for investment funds was already depressed.
"Recomposition of asset mix towards lower yielding investments will become inevitable, further compressing (profit) margins and hence (banking) sector earnings," the report said.
But commercial banks with big liquid funds could capitalise on the higher interbank rates, which would also benefit foreign and local banks with easy access to foreign currency deposits.
Foreign banks usually bring forex deposits from abroad and swap them with the central bank for rupees which they then lend to the corporate sector or use in the interbank money market.
KASB & Co said Tuesday's central bank offer of a 17 percent annual yield and other concessions to banks bringing in forex deposits would help the government and the banks.
It said the deposits would have no impact on the money supply or inflation as they would be held by the central bank, but would help shore up the depleting foreign exchange reserves position.
The central bank said foreign reserves stood at $756 million, excluding gold reserves of $800 million, on Tuesday, compared to $831 million on October 3.
